board.prose:
"Done." The clerk struck the figure, swept the goods off the counter into a woven basket behind her, and counted out the coin — a gold piece and two silver, stacked neatly and pushed across the wood to him. "Pleasure doing business. You bring clean work, I'll give you that. Most of the novices bring me skins still full of holes."

The coin went into his pouch, and it made a different sound in there now, heavier.

"The board's the same wall as ever," she said, tipping her pencil toward the far side of the hall. "Fresh notices went up this morning, if you want the pick of them."

The two murmuring adventurers had drifted off toward the door, and the board stood open to him. The notices were pinned in a tidy column, the Guild's standardized slips in their neat printed hands, and he read down them:

**Cull the Mud Viper at the Mill Wheel Shallows** — 45 cp · Kill 1 mud viper at the shallows below the mill wheel, Miller's Crossing. Client: Ostler Harn, ferry-keeper.

**Thin the Bog Striders at the Reed Flats Eel-Weirs** — 150 cp · Kill 6 bog striders at the eel-weirs of the Reed Flats, south of Glassmere. Client: the eel-fishers' association.

**Purge the Barrowfield Ghouls** — 300 cp · Kill 4 barrowfield ghouls at the old Barrowfield east of the north road. Client: Warden of the North Road, Glassmere.

**Slay the Ashveil Ridge Wyvern** — 550 cp · Kill 1 Ashveil Ridge wyvern at the high pastures of Ashveil Ridge above Glassmere. Client: the shepherds of the Ashveil high pastures.

**Clear Glimmerdeep Grotto, Level 1** — 60 cp · Clear level 1 of Glimmerdeep Grotto. Client: the Glassmere academy of magic. A note at the bottom of this one, in smaller script: *Groups and stronger foes; a matching rank does not guarantee a safe solo expedition.*

Morning light came through the high windows and lay across the board in long pale bars. Behind him, the clerk had gone back to her ledger, and somewhere deeper in the hall a door opened and closed, and boots crossed stone.

accept.prose:
The clerk took the slip down from the board, turned to her ledger, and ruled a line beneath the entry before she wrote his name against it. "Thin the bog striders. Reed Flats. Six of them, dead, at the eel-weirs." She stamped the slip, blew across the seal, and held it out. "Active as of now. Seal goes READY when the work's done — bring it back here and the desk pays you the hundred and fifty copper, nothing to argue over."

She leaned an elbow on the counter. "Word from the fishers is the striders have been working the weirs hard this spring, tearing the eel traps open for what's inside. So there'll be plenty of them where the traps are. They're quick on the mud and they spit, if you've not met one. Which you have, I'd guess." Her eyes flicked to the worn edge of his pouch. "Anyway. That's the whole of it."

The slip went into the pouch alongside its older twin — the cull contract from days past, already struck through and paid, kept out of habit more than anything. The new seal was still faintly warm from the stamp.

Outside, the morning had warmed a degree or two, and a cartload of wool was grinding past toward the south gate, the same direction as the flats. The Guild hall door stood open behind him, and the road to the Reed Flats lay downhill and south, past the wall.

founding.prose:
He ate what the healer put in front of him — smoked eel, barley, bread — and she watched until the bowl was empty, then let him take his staff and go, with a warning about the knee that followed him out the door.

The Guild hall sat at the village's landward end, a plank building on thicker poles with the white and blue painted fresh along its lintel. Inside, the smell was lamp oil and wet wool. A clerk sat behind the counter, a narrow woman with ink stains to her wrists, and a board of contract slips hung on the wall behind her. She looked up at his bound arm and bloody trouser leg and reached under the counter for the ledger without being asked.

He laid both contract slips on the counter.

She took the first, checked the seal, then flipped it over and set it back down. "Cull at the eel-weirs. Six called for." She tapped the ledger line. "Five on the roll. The slips take the count off the weirs' enchanted posts — the kill-markers don't lie and I can't close a slip short." She pulled the second one toward her, ran her thumb over the seal, and shook her head before he said anything. "Same work, same count. Five. Both of them want six."

She squared the slips and slid them back across the counter to him.

"You've done the hard part, by the look of you. The bed's marked you five and the sixth is owed. Kill one more strider at the weirs and both seals will show READY when you come back, and I'll pay you the three hundred copper on the spot — both contracts, both payouts, no argument." She was already reaching for the ink pot to note the visit. "Or if you're set on turning in short, I can't. Guild's strict on it and so am I."

turnin.prose:
The drying loft stair creaked under his boots in the grey of early morning. Below, the mill was already at work — the wheel knocking, water sluicing — and Ottery was nowhere in sight, his voice muffled somewhere inside the machinery of his own living. The flats lay under river mist, the sedge clumps dark islands again, and the gravel bar where the viper had died showed only as a paler smudge in the reek of the channel.

Alaric took the towpath east.

The morning carried him along it through thinning mist: towpath gravel, then a hedged lane, then the broader track where cart ruts ran deep from the autumn rains. A woman driving two geese with a stick stepped off the path to let him pass and gave him the flat look country people give armed strangers. A herd boy watched him from a gate, mouth open, and said nothing. The sun climbed and burned the mist off the reed beds, and by the time the stilt village showed ahead — its platforms on their posts above the water, walkways and drying racks and the Guild hall's hanging sign among them — the day had gone bright and ordinary.

The Guild hall stood on the largest platform, reached by a plank walk from the shore. Inside it smelled of lamp oil and wet rope. A clerk with ink-stained fingers sat behind the counter, and a sleepy-looking pair of adventurers occupied a bench by the wall, arguing over a map. The clerk looked up as Alaric approached.

"Business?"

The contract slip came out of his pouch, seal showing READY. The clerk took it, held it to the lamp for a moment, and touched the seal with one finger; the enchanted ink warmed and went from READY to COMPLETED in a slow bloom.

"Mud viper at the mill wheel shallows. Confirmed." He scratched a line into the roll beside him, then counted four copper from the till and set them on the counter in a tidy stack. "Forty copper, posted rate. Anything else for the desk?"

Behind Alaric, the two on the bench had stopped arguing and were looking at the slip and at him.
